title: Compound assignment
example:
local count = 10
count += 5
count -= 1
local flags = 0
flags |= 1 << 3
flags &= ~(1 << 3)
local stats = { kills = 0 }
stats.kills += 1
description: `v op= expr` is equivalent to `v = v op (expr)`: the whole right-hand side is evaluated first. Exactly nine operators exist. The target can be a local, upvalue, global, field or indexed element; for indexed targets the table and key are evaluated once. `/=` always produces a float.
pitfalls: `^=` is bitwise XOR, not exponentiation: with x = 3, `x ^= 2` gives 1. Write `x = x ^ 2` for a power.
`//=`, `%=` and `..=` do not exist.
Single target only: `a, b += 1, 1` is a syntax error.
It is a statement, not an expression: `print(a += 1)` does not compile.
The operator must be written without spaces: `a + = 1` is a syntax error.
The runtime does not protect `<const>` locals: `c += 1` on a constant is either ignored or really modifies it. Sensity DevKit reports it as an error.

title: Safe navigation
example:
local config = { vehicle = { plate = 'CFX 001' } }
local plate = config?.vehicle?.plate
local color = config?.paint?.primary
local upper = config.vehicle.plate?:upper()
local onDone = config.onDone
onDone?('finished')
description: When the value before `?` is nil or false, evaluation skips the rest of the whole suffix chain and the chain evaluates to that nil or false. Any other value continues normally. When a statement (call or assignment) starts with a chain that short-circuits, the entire statement is skipped, including its right-hand side.
pitfalls: Only nil and false short-circuit: indexing a number with `?.` still raises an error.
`a?.b.c` raises an error when `a` exists but `a.b` is nil; write `a?.b?.c`.
There is no `??` operator and no ternary `a ? b : c`; use `a or b` and `cond and x or y`.
In a multiple assignment only the first target may contain `?`.

title: In unpacking
syntax: local name1, name2 in source | name1, name2 in source
example:
local coords = { x = 215.7, y = -810.1, z = 30.7 }
local x, y, z in coords
local health, armour = 0, 0
health, armour in ({ health = 200, armour = 50 })
description: Declares (or assigns) variables from the fields of a table with the same names: `local x, y in t` is `local x, y = t.x, t.y`. The source is evaluated once. In the non-local form the key comes from each target: its name, its field name (`obj.name`) or its integer index (`obj[1]`).
pitfalls: The source must be a name, an index, a call or a parenthesized expression: `local a in { a = 1 }` is a syntax error, `local a in ({ a = 1 })` works.
Only one source expression is allowed.
The `<close>` attribute is silently ignored with `in`: the value is never closed.
Fields are read by name, not by position: `local a, b in { 10, 20 }` gives nil, nil.

title: Set constructors
example:
local allowedJobs = { .police, .ambulance, ['tow-truck'] }
if allowedJobs['police'] then
    print('allowed')
end
description: Inside a table constructor, `.name` without a value means `name = true` and `[expr]` without a value means `[expr] = true`. `.name = value` is accepted as an alternative spelling of `name = value`.
pitfalls: `{ .5 }` is the number 0.5, not a set entry.
Keywords cannot follow the dot: `{ .end }` is a syntax error; use `{ ['end'] }`.
Only a single name is allowed: `{ .a.b }` is a syntax error.

title: C-style block comments
description: Text between `/*` and the next `*/` is a comment and may span several lines.
pitfalls: Comments do not nest: the first `*/` ends the comment.
Newlines inside `/* */` are not counted by the runtime, so error messages after a multi-line C comment report wrong (too small) line numbers. Prefer `--[[ ]]`.
`//` is not a comment: it is integer division.
An unterminated `/*` is a syntax error.

title: Compile-time hashes
example:
local ADDER <const> = `adder`
local same = `adder` == `ADDER`
local unsigned = `adder` & 0xFFFFFFFF
RequestModel(`adder`)
description: A string between backticks is replaced at compile time by its Jenkins one-at-a-time hash (the GetHashKey hash), as a signed 32-bit integer. ASCII letters are lowercased before hashing. The result is a constant, usable with `<const>` and as a call argument.
pitfalls: The value is signed: hashes above 0x7FFFFFFF are negative. Use `& 0xFFFFFFFF` to display the unsigned form.
The literal must fit on one line.
For strings known only at runtime, use `joaat(str)` or `GetHashKey(str)`.

title: <const> locals
description: Standard Lua 5.4: a constant local cannot be assigned after its declaration. Assigning it with `=` is a compile error.
pitfalls: Compound assignment (`+=`, `-=`, ...) on a `<const>` local is not rejected by the runtime and behaves unpredictably. Sensity DevKit reports it.
Only the variable is constant: a `<const>` table can still have its fields modified.

title: <close> locals and defer()
example:
do
    local _ <close> = defer(function()
        print('cleanup')
    end)
    print('work')
end
description: Standard Lua 5.4: when the variable goes out of scope (normally or because of an error), the value's `__close` metamethod is called. The CfxLua global `defer(fn)` returns a value whose `__close` calls `fn`.
pitfalls: The value must have a `__close` metamethod, or be nil or false; otherwise an error is raised.
`<close>` combined with `in` unpacking is silently ignored.
There is no `defer ... end` statement in CfxLua; use `defer(function() ... end)`.

title: Integer division and bitwise operators
syntax: a // b | a & b | a | b | a ~ b | ~a | a << n | a >> n
example:
local half = 7 // 2
local FLAG_A <const> = 1 << 0
local FLAG_B <const> = 1 << 1
local state = FLAG_A | FLAG_B
local hasB = (state & FLAG_B) ~= 0
state = state & ~FLAG_A
description: Standard Lua 5.4: `//` is floor division, `/` always returns a float, and `& | ~ << >>` are bitwise operators on integers (`~` is XOR between two operands and NOT as a unary operator).
pitfalls: `~=` is the not-equal operator; `~` alone is XOR or NOT.
`//` is not a comment.
Bitwise operators require integer-representable numbers: `1.5 & 1` raises an error.

title: Vector and quaternion types
syntax: vector2(x, y) | vector3(x, y, z) | vector4(x, y, z, w) | vec(...) | quat(...)
example:
local a = vector3(1, 2, 3)
local b = a + vector3(0, 0, 1)
local flat = a.xy
local length = #a
local x, y, z = table.unpack(a)
description: Runtime value types rather than syntax: `type(v)` is 'vector2', 'vector3', 'vector4' or 'quat'. Components are read with x/y/z/w, r/g/b/a or 1..4; multi-letter swizzles such as `v.zyx` build new vectors; `#v` is the length; arithmetic works component-wise.
pitfalls: Vectors are immutable: `v.x = 1` raises an error; build a new vector.
Multi-letter swizzles only accept x, y, z, w: `v.rgb` is nil.
`#v` is the magnitude, not the number of components (use `v.n`).
Components are 32-bit floats.

title: No ++ or -- operators
description: CfxLua has no increment or decrement operator. `i++` and `++i` are syntax errors. `--` always starts a comment, so `i--` compiles as the expression `i` followed by a comment.
pitfalls: `local x = i-- 1` silently compiles as `local x = i`: the rest of the line is a comment.
`a--=1` is a comment, while `a-=1` is a compound subtraction.

title: Syntax from other languages that does not exist
syntax: not supported: != | ! | ?? | a ? b : c | => | continue | //= | %= | ..= | // comment | defer ... end
example:
local a, b = 1, 2
local different = a ~= b
local negated = not different
local value = nil
local fallback = value or 'default'
local label = different and 'yes' or 'no'
local double = function(x) return x * 2 end
for i = 1, 3 do
    if i == 2 then goto continue end
    print(i)
    ::continue::
end
description: Use `~=` for not-equal, `not` for negation, `or` / `and ... or` instead of `??` and the ternary operator, `function` instead of arrow functions, `goto continue` with a `::continue::` label instead of `continue`, explicit assignments instead of `//=`, `%=`, `..=`, `--` comments instead of `//` comments, and `defer(fn)` with `<close>` instead of a defer statement.
pitfalls: `cond and a or b` returns b when a is false or nil.
`x // comment` divides `x` by a variable named `comment`.
